agency_full: European Space Agency (lead, spacecraft + 6 instruments) / National Aeronautics and Space Administration (launch + DSN + RTG power + 3 instruments)
payload: 366 kg spin-stabilised, 9 instruments (magnetometer, solar wind, energetic particles, radio + plasma waves, dust, cosmic rays, gamma-ray burst detector, solar-wind composition, X-ray + gamma-ray bursts). Powered by a single GPHS-RTG.
delta_v: ~15.4 km/s (Jupiter gravity assist did the heavy lifting)
credit: © ESA / NASA / Ulysses. Ulysses launched 1990-10-06 from STS-41 Discovery — the only spacecraft ever placed into a high-inclination heliocentric orbit. To reach a near-polar Sun-relative orbit (~80° inclination) from Earth's near-equatorial orbital plane requires impractical chemical ΔV, so Ulysses used a Jupiter gravity assist (1992-02-08) to deflect itself out of the ecliptic. The spacecraft completed three full polar orbits of the Sun over 18.5 years, mapping the solar wind, heliospheric magnetic field, and energetic particle environments at all heliographic latitudes — the only direct measurements ever made of how solar-wind structure varies between the equatorial slow-wind regions and the high-latitude fast-wind streams from coronal holes. Key findings: fast solar wind (~750 km/s) fills high latitudes during solar minimum and contracts to coronal holes near the equator at solar maximum; cosmic-ray flux at high latitudes is unexpectedly modest; interstellar dust enters the heliosphere from the ecliptic plane. Mission terminated 2009-06-30 when telemetry hydrazine froze in the cooling thruster lines. Hardware remains in heliocentric polar orbit.

events.label: Launch — STS-41 Discovery / IUS+PAM-S
events.description: Cape Canaveral, 1990-10-06. Joint ESA / NASA mission, deployed from Space Shuttle Discovery and accelerated by a two-stage upper stage (Inertial Upper Stage + Payload Assist Module-S) — the fastest spacecraft ever launched at the time (40 km/s relative to Earth on a Jupiter escape trajectory).

events.label: Jupiter — out-of-ecliptic gravity assist
events.description: Closest approach 380,000 km from Jupiter on 1992-02-08. The encounter was used for one purpose: bend Ulysses's trajectory ~80° out of the ecliptic plane, an angle no chemical rocket could deliver from Earth directly. The flyby left Ulysses on a polar solar orbit — the only spacecraft ever to study the Sun's poles.

events.label: First south polar pass
events.description: September 1994. Ulysses passed over the Sun's south solar pole for the first time, mapping the polar magnetic field structure + the high-speed solar wind streaming from the polar coronal holes. The solar minimum conditions made for a 'clean' polar wind sample.

events.label: First north polar pass
events.description: July 1995. Companion to the south polar pass, this time over the northern solar pole. The two passes together delivered the first true 3D map of the heliosphere — confirming the Sun's polar magnetic-field structure flips during solar maximum (a finding Ulysses confirmed in its second polar pass set, 2000-2001).

events.label: End of mission — propellant frozen
events.description: 2009-06-30. Ulysses was decommissioned after 18 years of operation — far beyond the planned 5-year mission. The cause was thermal: as the RTG decayed below the threshold needed to keep hydrazine propellant lines warm, the propellant would have frozen and the spacecraft become unrecoverable. Three polar pass sets had been completed by then; the heliospheric data archive remains the standard reference.
